newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens to buy, sell units to up profit.
newsitem.headline: Siemens to buy, sell units to up profit.

text.p: German industrial giant Siemems AG plans to step up its already brisk pace of acquisitions and sell-offs as part a drive to put profit back on course for growth.

Siemens businesses unlikely to reach a goal of 15 percent return on capital by the year 2000 could be targeted for disposal in a plan to unload units with business volume of about 3.5 billion marks ($2.1 billion) this year, finance chief Karl-Hermann Baumann told Reuters on Thursday.

"The performance of the units is being checked in comparison to their yield on assigned assets," Baumann said without naming specific businesses. "There are several units that stand below the formulated profit goals now."
At the same time, Siemens was searching for possible acquisitions in high-tech growth businesses and in parts of the world that are growing faster than Germany, Baumann said.
Acquisitions would help drive revenue, which could rise 50 percent to 150 billion marks in five years, Baumann said.

Analysts said Siemens' medical technology group, which forecast a loss this year after a profitable 1995/96, could come under increased scrutiny in the sell-off drive, but they expected most activity in small groups within Siemens units.
"It will probably be a lot of things we don't hear much about," said one Siemens analyst who declined to be named. "You're going to see a stream of small deals, not big ones."

The German weekly Der Spiegel on Thursday reported Siemens might sell off small groups that produce sugar and paper processing equipment. Last month the company closed down a small unit that made TVs.

Other major groups standing short of profit targets are the transportation technology group, which also forecast a 1996/97 loss, and Siemens Nixdorf Informationssysteme AG, the computer unit that was just barely profitable last year.
Siemens has begun talking to possible buyers of its cable television network, spokesman Eberhard Dombek confirmed.

"We are putting our portfolio to the test," Dombek said. "We have always done that but now we are doing it more intensively. We are asking whether we can be successful with businesses long term. If we can't, then we intend to sell them or put them into joint ventures."

Siemens, whose shares rose 1.62 marks to 85 marks in Thursday afternoon electronic trading, has come under pressure to increase profit since it warned in November profit would not improve in the 1996/97 business year.
On the warning, its shares fell nine percent to 72 marks.

On the acquisitions front, Siemens' public and private telecommunications groups have already outlined ambitious plans to grow in large part by buying into new businesses, especially businesses in Asia and North America.
"There is a strategy and we know what areas we want to strengthen," Dombek said.
